claim: Acid-sensing ion channels (ASICs) are trimeric cation-selective channels activated by decreases in extracellular pH.
source: Acid-sensing ion channels (ASICs) are trimeric cation-selective channels activated by decreases in extracellular pH.
evidence: This is a well-established characterization of ASICs supported by scientific consensus.

claim: The intracellular N and C terminal tails of ASIC1 influence channel gating, trafficking, and signaling in ischemic cell death.
source: The intracellular N and C terminal tails of ASIC1 influence channel gating, trafficking, and signaling in ischemic cell death.
evidence: This statement is supported by references to prior work in the field.

claim: Several X-ray and cryo-EM structures of the extracellular and transmembrane segments of ASIC1 have been determined, but the intracellular tails remain unresolved.
source: Despite several X-ray and cryo-EM structures of the extracellular and transmembrane segments of ASIC1, these important intracellular tails remain unresolved.
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies (Baconguis et al., 2014; Gonzales et al., 2009; Yoder and Gouaux, 2020; Yoder et al., 2018) mentioned in the Introduction.

claim: The C terminal tail of chicken ASIC1 projects into the cytosol by approximately 35 Å.
source: We find the C terminal tail projects into the cytosol by approximately 35 Å
evidence: This is a primary finding from the DPA quenching experiments reported in the manuscript.

claim: The N and C tails from the same subunits are closer than adjacent subunits.
source: We find the C terminal tail projects into the cytosol by approximately 35 Å and that the N and C tails from the same subunits are closer than adjacent subunits.
evidence: This is supported by FLIM FRET measurements comparing intra- versus inter-subunit distances.

claim: Using pH-insensitive fluorescent proteins, no relative movement between the N and C tails upon extracellular acidification was detected.
source: Using pH-insensitive fluorescent proteins, we fail to detect any relative movement between the N and C tails upon extracellular acidification
evidence: This is based on patch clamp fluorometry experiments with GFP-RFP pairs.

claim: Axial motions of the membrane proximal segments toward the plasma membrane occur upon extracellular acidification.
source: Using pH-insensitive fluorescent proteins, we fail to detect any relative movement between the N and C tails upon extracellular acidification but do observe axial motions of the membrane proximal segments toward the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is supported by DPA quenching experiments at different pH values.

claim: ASICs are the predominant sensor of extracellular pH in the central and peripheral nervous system.
source: The predominant sensor of extracellular pH in the central and peripheral nervous system is thought to be acid-sensing ion channels (ASICs) (Pattison et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pattison et al., 2019.

claim: ASICs couple extracellular acidification to synaptic transmission and plasticity.
source: This family of trimeric pH-activated sodium-selective ion channels couples extracellular acidification to numerous physiological and pathophysiological consequences including synaptic transmission and plasticity (Du et al., 2014; Kreple et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2016; Uchitel et al., 2019; Yu et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: ASICs are involved in fear memory consolidation and expression.
source: This family of trimeric pH-activated sodium-selective ion channels couples extracellular acidification to numerous physiological and pathophysiological consequences including synaptic transmission and plasticity (Du et al., 2014; Kreple et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2016; Uchitel et al., 2019; Yu et al., 2018), fear memory consolidation and expression (Du et al., 2017; Taugher et al., 2020; Taugher et al., 2017; Taugher et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: ASICs are involved in epilepsy.
source: This family of trimeric pH-activated sodium-selective ion channels couples extracellular acidification to numerous physiological and pathophysiological consequences including synaptic transmission and plasticity (Du et al., 2014; Kreple et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2016; Uchitel et al., 2019; Yu et al., 2018), fear memory consolidation and expression (Du et al., 2017; Taugher et al., 2020; Taugher et al., 2017; Taugher et al., 2014), epilepsy (Ziemann et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ziemann et al., 2008.

claim: ASICs are involved in ischemia-induced cell death.
source: This family of trimeric pH-activated sodium-selective ion channels couples extracellular acidification to numerous physiological and pathophysiological consequences including synaptic transmission and plasticity (Du et al., 2014; Kreple et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2016; Uchitel et al., 2019; Yu et al., 2018), fear memory consolidation and expression (Du et al., 2017; Taugher et al., 2020; Taugher et al., 2017; Taugher et al., 2014), epilepsy (Ziemann et al., 2008), and ischemia-induced cell death (Wemmie et al., 2013; Xiong et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wemmie et al., 2013 and Xiong et al., 2004.

claim: Most ASIC subunits desensitize nearly completely in a few seconds.
source: Since most ASIC subunits desensitize nearly completely in a few seconds (Benson et al., 2002; Gründer and Pusch, 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Benson et al., 2002 and Gründer and Pusch, 2015.

claim: ASICs possess both canonical ionic and non-canonical metabotropic signaling capabilities.
source: While other extracellular pH sensors may play roles (Pattison et al., 2019; Ruan et al., 2020), recent evidence reveals that ASICs possess both canonical ionic and non-canonical metabotropic signaling capabilities.
evidence: This is supported by citations and recent evidence.

claim: Extracellular acidosis drives the association of RIP1 and N-ethylmaleimide-sensitive factor with ASIC1a, triggering RIP1 phosphorylation and initiating a necroptotic signaling cascade.
source: Extracellular acidosis is proposed to drive the association of the serine/threonine kinase receptor interacting protein 1 (RIP1) and N-ethylmaleimide-sensitive factor with ASIC1a, triggering RIP1 phosphorylation and initiating a necroptotic signaling cascade (Wang et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2020 and Wang et al., 2015.

claim: The ASIC1a-mediated necroptotic signaling occurs independent of ASIC1a ion conductance and via intracellular protein-protein interactions.
source: This occurs independent of ASIC1a ion conductance and via intracellular protein-protein interactions (Wang et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2020 and Wang et al., 2015.

claim: The structure of the ASIC extracellular and transmembrane regions has been determined.
source: Like many of these ion channels, the structure of the ASIC extracellular and transmembrane regions has been determined (Baconguis et al., 2014; Gonzales et al., 2009; Yoder and Gouaux, 2020; Yoder et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to structural studies.

claim: The intracellular domains of ASICs are unresolved in structural studies.
source: Like many of these ion channels, the structure of the ASIC extracellular and transmembrane regions has been determined (Baconguis et al., 2014; Gonzales et al., 2009; Yoder and Gouaux, 2020; Yoder et al., 2018), but the intracellular domains (ICDs) are unresolved.
evidence: This is supported by the absence of ICD structures in cited studies.

claim: The ASIC ICDs are likely partly or mostly unstructured regions.
source: It is likely that the ASIC ICDs are partly, or even mostly, unstructured regions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of resolved structures.

claim: The short (15 amino acid) N tail projects about 6–10 Å from the membrane inner leaflet into the cytosol.
source: We find that the short (15 amino acid) N tail projects about 6–10 Å from the membrane inner leaflet into the cytosol
evidence: This is based on DPA quenching measurements and modeling.

claim: The longer 67 amino acid C tail extends between 30 and 40 Å.
source: We find that the short (15 amino acid) N tail projects about 6–10 Å from the membrane inner leaflet into the cytosol while the longer 67 amino acid C tail extends between 30 and 40 Å.
evidence: This is based on DPA quenching measurements and modeling.

claim: The ASIC C tail orientation contrasts with the unresolved tail of AMPA receptors that is largely perpendicular to the membrane.
source: This contrasts with the unresolved tail of AMPA receptors that is largely perpendicular to the membrane (Zachariassen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a comparison supported by a citation to Zachariassen et al., 2016.

claim: The N and proximal segment of the C tail from the same subunits are closer than adjacent subunits, suggesting preferential intra-subunit tail interactions.
source: We also report that the N and proximal segment of the C tail from the same subunits are closer than adjacent subunits, suggesting preferential intra-subunit tail interactions which may inform the interpretation of experiments with heteromeric channels.
evidence: This is based on FLIM FRET data comparing intra- and inter-subunit distances.

claim: The intracellular components of the cASIC1 N and C terminal tails are 15 and 67 amino acids, respectively.
source: The intracellular components of the cASIC1 N and C terminal tails are 15 and 67 amino acids, respectively.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the construct used.

claim: DPA is a dark acceptor, allowing FRET to be easily measured by changes in donor emission.
source: First, it is a dark acceptor, allowing FRET to be easily measured by changes in donor emission.
evidence: This is a known property of DPA supported by prior literature.

claim: DPA binds and dissociates from the plasma membrane quickly with respect to the time of a patch clamp experiment.
source: Second, it binds and dissociates from the plasma membrane quickly with respect to the time of a patch clamp experiment.
evidence: This is a known property of DPA supported by prior literature.

claim: The anionic DPA orients in the plasma membrane depending on voltage, being pulled into the inner membrane leaflet by depolarization or pushed to the outer leaflet by hyperpolarization.
source: Third, and most critically, the anionic DPA orients in the plasma membrane depending on voltage, being pulled into the inner membrane leaflet by depolarization or pushed to the outer leaflet by hyperpolarization.
evidence: This is a known property of DPA supported by prior literature.

claim: Voltage steps can move DPA molecules closer to, or further from, the donor by a fixed distance of 25 Å, reflecting the estimated displacement of DPA.
source: Thus, voltage steps can move DPA molecules closer to, or further from, the donor by a fixed distance of 25 Å, reflecting to the estimated displacement of DPA (Wang et al., 2010; Zachariassen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2010 and Zachariassen et al., 2016.

claim: Lck-CFP gave robust voltage-dependent fluorescence changes in the presence of DPA (5 µM) but not in its absence.
source: Membrane tethered CFP (Lck-CFP) gave robust voltage-dependent fluorescence changes in the presence of DPA (5 µM) but not in its absence and was quantified as the difference between the top and bottom values of a Boltzmann sigmoidal fit of the normalized fluorescence (ΔF/F−15 mv = 0.45 ± 0.03, n = 6, Figure 1C & D)
evidence: This is based on patch clamp fluorometry data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Lck-CFP quenching (ΔF/F−15 mv = 0.45 ± 0.03, n = 6) is consistent with the fluorophore being close to the plasma membrane and having a relatively high R0 distance (47 Å).
source: Membrane tethered CFP (Lck-CFP) gave robust voltage-dependent fluorescence changes in the presence of DPA (5 µM) but not in its absence and was quantified as the difference between the top and bottom values of a Boltzmann sigmoidal fit of the normalized fluorescence (ΔF/F−15 mv = 0.45 ± 0.03, n = 6, Figure 1C & D), consistent with the fluorophore being close to the plasma membrane and having a relatively high R0 distance (47 Å).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data based on FRET theory.

claim: Lck-YFP gave relatively weak voltage-dependent quenching in the presence of DPA (ΔF/F−15 mv = 0.16 ± 0.013, n = 6).
source: The Lck-YFP gave relatively weak voltage-dependent quenching in the presence of DPA (ΔF/F−15 mv = 0.16 ± 0.013, n = 6, Figure 1C & D)
evidence: This is based on patch clamp fluorometry data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Lck-YFP quenching is consistent with a membrane proximal position but relatively lower R0 distance (36.5 Å).
source: The Lck-YFP gave relatively weak voltage-dependent quenching in the presence of DPA (ΔF/F−15 mv = 0.16 ± 0.013, n = 6, Figure 1C & D), which is also consistent with a membrane proximal position but relatively lower R0 distance (36.5 Å).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data based on FRET theory.

claim: FP insertions did not disrupt channel function as determined by the rates of desensitization and recovery, although small differences in desensitization decay of C4 and recovery of C1 insertions appeared.
source: Importantly, FP insertions did not disrupt channel function as determined by the rates of desensitization and recovery, although small differences in desensitization decay of C4 and recovery of C1 insertions appeared (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The FP-tagged ASIC1 constructs showed robust plasma membrane localization in confocal microscopy.
source: Further, these constructs showed robust plasma membrane localization in confocal microscopy (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on confocal imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: With CFP insertions, the C1 position gave the strongest quenching (ΔF/F−15 mv = 0.65 ± 0.03).
source: Specifically, we found that with CFP insertions, the C1 position gave the strongest quenching (ΔF/F−15 mv = 0.65 ± 0.03)
evidence: This is based on DPA quenching measurements.

claim: With CFP insertions, N and C2 positions gave about equal quenching (ΔF/F−15 mv = 0.48 ± 0.03 and ΔF/F−15 mv = 0.51 ± 0.05).
source: Specifically, we found that with CFP insertions, the C1 position gave the strongest quenching (ΔF/F−15 mv = 0.65 ± 0.03) with N and C2 being about equal (ΔF/F−15 mv = 0.48 ± 0.03 and ΔF/F−15 mv = 0.51 ± 0.05)
evidence: This is based on DPA quenching measurements.

claim: With CFP insertions, C3 and C4 had progressively less quenching (ΔF/F−15 mv = 0.39 ± 0.03 and ΔF/F−15 mv = 0.21 ± 0.03).
source: Specifically, we found that with CFP insertions, the C1 position gave the strongest quenching (ΔF/F−15 mv = 0.65 ± 0.03) with N and C2 being about equal (ΔF/F−15 mv = 0.48 ± 0.03 and ΔF/F−15 mv = 0.51 ± 0.05) and C3 and C4 having progressively less quenching (ΔF/F−15 mv = 0.39 ± 0.03 and ΔF/F−15 mv = 0.21 ± 0.03).
evidence: This is based on DPA quenching measurements.

claim: With YFP insertions, the N terminal YFP gave the strongest quenching (ΔF/F−15 mv = 0.26 ± 0.02).
source: In the case of YFP, a slightly different pattern was observed where the N terminal YFP gave the strongest quenching (ΔF/F−15 mv = 0.26 ± 0.02)
evidence: This is based on DPA quenching measurements.

claim: With YFP insertions, C1–C4 gave progressively weaker quenching (ΔF/F−15 mv between 0.23 ± 0.02 and 0.14 ± 0.01).
source: In the case of YFP, a slightly different pattern was observed where the N terminal YFP gave the strongest quenching (ΔF/F−15 mv = 0.26 ± 0.02) with C1–C4 giving progressively weaker quenching (ΔF/F−15 mv between 0.23 ± 0.02 and 0.14 ± 0.01, Figure 2B–D).
evidence: This is based on DPA quenching measurements shown in Figure 2.

claim: Quenching of the N terminal YFP insertion was statistically distinguishable from the C4 insertion (p = 0.019).
source: Quenching of the N terminal YFP insertion was statistically distinguishable from the C4 insertion (p = 0.019) but did not detect differences between adjacent insertions as for CFP (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of DPA quenching data.

claim: The most parsimonious interpretation of the DPA quenching data is that the N terminal insertion point is membrane proximal while all positions in the C tail are progressively further from the membrane.
source: The most parsimonious interpretation of these data is that the N terminal insertion point is membrane proximal while all positions in the C tail are progressively further from the membrane.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the pattern of quenching data.

claim: The tip of the N terminus is about 6–10 Å from the inner leaflet.
source: With this assumption, the strongest interpretation of our data is that the tip of the N terminus is about 6–10 Å from the inner leaflet
evidence: This is based on modeling of DPA quenching data with the assumption that the FP adds 10 Å to the axial distance.

claim: The C1 insertion site is approximately 12–16 Å away from the inner leaflet.
source: With this assumption, the strongest interpretation of our data is that the tip of the N terminus is about 6–10 Å from the inner leaflet while the C1 insertion site is approximately 12–16 Å away.
evidence: This is based on modeling of DPA quenching data with the assumption that the FP adds 10 Å to the axial distance.

claim: The final C terminal amino acids are likely within 30–40 Å of the inner leaflet.
source: Distance estimates for the C2–C4 insertion sites are difficult to assign; however, given that the C4 position shows quenching for both FPs, this final C terminal amino acids are likely within 30–40 Å of the inner leaflet.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of quenching at the C4 position.

claim: The C-α to C-α distance from the critical His74 to Lys355, at the base of thumb domain's alpha5 helix, is 35 Å in the resting state (PDB:6VTL).
source: For reference, the C-α to C-α distance from the critical His74 to Lys355, at the base of thumb domain's alpha5 helix, is 35 Å (Figure 2—figure supplement 6, resting state, PDB:6VTL).
evidence: This is a measurement from a published structure.

claim: A cluster of lysine and arginine residues (amino acids 461–476) in the membrane proximal segment of the C tail is proposed to interact with a segment of negatively charged amino acids in the N termini (amino acids 7–12), forming a salt bridge between the intracellular tails of the same subunit.
source: Within the membrane proximal segment of the C tail is a cluster of lysine and arginine residues (amino acids 461–476). These have been proposed to interact with a segment of negatively charged amino acids in the N termini (amino acids 7–12), forming a salt bridge between the intracellular tails of the same subunit (Wang et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2020 and Wang et al., 2015.

claim: CFP-cA1-YFP alone produced very strong FRET as evidenced by dramatically faster CFP lifetimes compared to N CFP (N CFP: 4.06 ± 0.02 ns, n = 76; CFP-cA1-YFP: 2.68 ± 0.03, n = 58).
source: As expected, CFP-cA1-YFP alone produced very strong FRET as evidenced by the dramatically faster CFP lifetimes compared to N CFP (N CFP: 4.06 ± 0.02 ns, n = 76; CFP-cA1-YFP: 2.68 ± 0.03, n = 58, Figure 3).
evidence: This is based on FLIM measurements shown in Figure 3.

claim: Adding more wild-type cASIC1 to CFP-cA1-YFP led to an increase in CFP lifetimes until reaching a plateau of approximately 3 ns, representing a FRET efficiency of 25% between CFP and YFP in a single subunit.
source: Adding more wild-type cASIC1 led to an increase in CFP lifetimes until reaching a plateau of approximately 3 ns, representing a FRET efficiency of 25% between CFP and YFP in a single subunit (1:31 ratio: 3.08 ± 0.03, n = 34, 24% FRET efficiency, Figure 3C).
evidence: This is based on FLIM measurements at varying cDNA ratios shown in Figure 3.

claim: Co-transfection of CFP-cA1-cA1 along with C4 YFP at increasing ratios produced progressively faster lifetimes up to about 3.3 ns or 15% FRET efficiency.
source: Co-transfection of CFP-cA1-cA1 along with C4 YFP at increasing ratios produced progressively faster lifetimes up to about 3.3 ns or 15% FRET efficiency (1:15: 3.28 ± 0.05 ns, n = 43, Figure 3).
evidence: This is based on FLIM measurements shown in Figure 3.

claim: The FRET efficiency from FPs on neighboring subunits (15 ± 1%, n = 43 for CFP-cA1-cA1 + C4 YFP 1:15) is significantly less than that observed in the CFP-cA1-YFP experiment (24 ± 1%, n = 46 for CFP-cA1-YFP + wild type 1:15, p < 1e−6).
source: Even with a 1:15 ratio of CFP-cA1-cA1 to C4 YFP, where all dimers likely have a C4 YFP monomer partner, the FRET efficiency is significantly less than that observed in the CFP-cA1-YFP experiment (15 ± 1%, n = 43 for CFP-cA1-cA1 + C4 YFP 1:15; 24 ± 1%, n = 46 for CFP-cA1-YFP + wild type 1:15, p < 1e−6, Student's t-test).
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of FLIM data.

claim: FPs on the same subunit show more efficient FRET than on different subunits, suggesting the tails of the same subunit are physically closer and more likely to associate.
source: Thus, FPs on the same subunit show more efficient FRET than on different subunits, suggesting the tails of the same subunit are physically closer and more likely to associate.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the FLIM FRET data.

claim: The putative salt bridge between the N terminal tail and the membrane proximal segment of the C tail is proposed to break apart to facilitate ion-independent signaling.
source: The putative salt bridge between the N terminal tail and the membrane proximal segment of the C tail is proposed to break apart to facilitate ion-independent signaling (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2020.

claim: Rapid application of pH 7 or 6, but not pH 8, produced a decrease in the ratio of YFP to CFP emission (i.e. change in FRET) with a slow time course (ΔFYFP/CFP pH 7: −2.6 ± 0.3%, n = 8, p = 0.031 versus pH 8; pH 6: −4.6 ± 0.5%, n = 8, p = 0.0025 versus pH 8).
source: As seen in Figure 4A and B, rapid application of pH 7 or 6, but not pH 8, produced a decrease in the ratio of YFP to CFP emission (i.e. change in FRET) with a slow time course (ΔFYFP/CFP pH 7: −2.6 ± 0.3%, n = 8, p = 0.031 versus pH 8; pH 6: −4.6 ± 0.5%, n = 8, p = 0.0025 versus pH 8).
evidence: This is based on patch clamp fluorometry data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The strong pH sensitivity of YFP complicates the interpretation of FRET measurements upon acidification.
source: However, as discussed previously (Wang et al., 2020), the strong pH sensitivity of YFP complicates the interpretation of these measurements.
evidence: This is a known property of YFP supported by prior literature.

claim: C4 YFP showed a strong loss of emission upon extracellular acidification (ΔFYFP pH 7: −2.6 ± 0.8%, n = 5; pH 6: −12 ± 2%, n = 8).
source: Consistent with this (Wang et al., 2020), we also observed a strong loss of emission from C4 YFP upon extracellular acidification (Figure 4A and B, ΔFYFP pH 7: −2.6 ± 0.8%, n = 5; pH 6: −12 ± 2%, n = 8).
evidence: This is based on patch clamp fluorometry data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The N CFP showed no change in emission upon extracellular acidification owing to this CFP variant's pKa of 3.1.
source: In contrast, the N CFP showed no such change in emission (Figure 4) owing to this CFP variants pKa of 3.1 (Goedhart et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on patch clamp fluorometry data and a citation to Goedhart et al., 2012.

claim: A novel GFP with a distinct chromophore and pKa of 3.4 was described.
source: Fortunately, a novel GFP was described with a distinct chromophore and pKa of 3.4 (Shinoda et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Shinoda et al., 2018.

claim: TagRFP has a relatively low pKa of 3.8.
source: When combined with a relatively low pKa red FP (TagRFP, pKa 3.8 Merzlyak et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Merzlyak et al., 2007.

claim: Both GFP-cA1 and cA1-RFP clones showed no change in their fluorescence emission with extracellular pH 6, 7, or 8.
source: As seen in Figure 4C and D, both clones showed no change in their fluorescence emission with extracellular pH 6, 7, or 8, confirming their suitability for measuring conformational changes induced by pH.
evidence: This is based on patch clamp fluorometry data shown in Figure 4.

claim: No change in the RFP/GFP ratio (i.e. no change in FRET) was detected from GFP-cA1-RFP upon acidification (ΔFRFP/GFP pH 7: −1.3± 0.5%; pH 6: −0.1 ± 0.6%, n = 5).
source: However, we detected no change in the RFP/GFP ratio (i.e. no change in FRET) from these FPs (Figure 4C and D, ΔFRFP/GFP pH 7: −1.3± 0.5%; pH 6: −0.1 ± 0.6%, n = 5).
evidence: This is based on patch clamp fluorometry data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The GFP does FRET with the RFP as the ratio of red to green fluorescence emission was significantly greater in the GFP-cA1-RFP clone compared to the GFP-cA1 only (GFP-cA1: 0.14 ± 0.01, n = 6; GFP-cA1-RFP: 0.41 ± 0.04, n = 7, p = 0.0014).
source: Importantly, the GFP does FRET with the RFP as the ratio of red to green fluorescence emission was significantly greater in the GFP-cA1-RFP clone compared to the GFP-cA1 only (GFP-cA1: 0.14 ± 0.01, n = 6; GFP-cA1-RFP: 0.41 ± 0.04, n = 7, p = 0.0014).
evidence: This is based on fluorescence measurements.

claim: No change in RFP/GFP ratio was detected with GFP-cA1-C1-RFP alone or when diluting this construct with unlabeled wild-type cASIC1 (ΔFRFP/GFP GFP-cA1-C1-RFP pH 6: −0.9 ± 1.4%, n = 3; + wild type pH 6: −0.8 ± 1.5%, n = 5).
source: Unfortunately, here again we did not detect any change in RFP/GFP ratio with either GFP-cA1-C1-RFP alone or when diluting this construct out with unlabeled wild-type cASIC1 (ΔFRFP/GFP GFP-cA1-C1-RFP pH 6: −0.9 ± 1.4%, n = 3; + wild type pH 6: −0.8 ± 1.5%, n = 5; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on patch clamp fluorometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The voltage-dependent quenching of Lck-CFP was not different between extracellular pH 8 compared to pH 6 (ΔF/F−15 mV pH 8: 0.45 ± 0.03, pH 6: 0.43 ± 0.04, n = 6, uncorrected p-value = 0.52).
source: Importantly, the voltage-dependent quenching of Lck-CFP was not different between extracellular pH 8 compared to pH 6 (ΔF/F−15 mV pH 8: 0.45 ± 0.03, pH 6: 0.43 ± 0.04, n = 6, uncorrected p-value = 0.52, paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test, Figure 5)
evidence: This is based on DPA quenching measurements at different pH values shown in Figure 5.

claim: The extent of quenching at the N and C1 position was significantly reduced in pH 6 compared to pH 8.
source: Interestingly, the extent of quenching at the N and C1 position was significantly reduced in pH 6 compared to pH 8 (Figure 5).
evidence: This is based on DPA quenching measurements at different pH values shown in Figure 5.

claim: In the resting state (pH 8), CFP at the N or C1 position had a ΔF/F−15 mV of 0.49 ± 0.02 or 0.57 ± 0.04 (n = 13 or 11), respectively.
source: Specifically, in the resting state (pH 8), CFP at the N or C1 position had a ΔF/F−15 mV of 0.49 ± 0.02 or 0.57 ± 0.04 (n = 13 or 11), respectively.
evidence: This is based on DPA quenching measurements.

claim: With extracellular pH 6 (populating the desensitized state), the ΔF/F−15 mV at N and C1 positions were reduced to 0.41 ± 0.02 and 0.55 ± 0.03.
source: However, with extracellular pH 6 (populating the desensitized state), these were reduced to 0.41 ± 0.02 and 0.55 ± 0.03.
evidence: This is based on DPA quenching measurements.

claim: The effect of pH on the extent of quenching at the N position was readily reversible.
source: In a subset of cells expressing the N CFP clone, we maintained the recording in pH 8, 6 and then back to pH 8 and found the effect on the extent of quenching was readily reversible (Figure 5D–E).
evidence: This is based on DPA quenching measurements shown in Figure 5D-E.

claim: None of the other positions (C2, C3, C4) showed significant evidence of movement between pH 8 and pH 6 conditions.
source: None of the other positions showed significant evidence of movement between these conditions (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1), supporting that this motion is specific to the membrane proximal region and not a general pH artifact.
evidence: This is based on DPA quenching measurements shown in Figure 5.

claim: Both the N and C tails of cASIC1 move axially with respect to the membrane between the resting and desensitized states.
source: These results demonstrate that both the N and C tails of cASIC1 move axially with respect to the membrane between the resting and desensitized states.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the DPA quenching data at different pH values.

claim: The reduced quenching at the N position in the pH 6 condition indicates the FP moves closer to the plasma membrane upon channel desensitization.
source: The reduced quenching in the pH 6 condition indicates the FP moves even closer to the plasma membrane upon channel desensitization.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the DPA quenching data and theoretical modeling.

claim: The data favor a model where the N and proximal segment of the C tail move up toward the inner membrane leaflet when the channel is exposed to desensitizing conditions.
source: Therefore, our data favor a model where the N and proximal segment of the C tail move up toward the inner membrane leaflet when the channel is exposed to desensitizing conditions (Figure 6).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the DPA quenching data at different pH values, illustrated in Figure 6.

claim: Structures of full-length cASIC1 have been solved using cryo-EM, but the N and C tails give no resolvable density.
source: Structures of full-length cASIC1 have been solved using cryo-EM. The N and C tails are present in these constructs yet give no resolvable density (Yoder and Gouaux, 2020; Yoder et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yoder and Gouaux, 2020 and Yoder et al., 2018.

claim: The lack of resolvable density for the tails suggests they may be largely disordered.
source: This suggests the tails maybe largely disordered, waiting to bind intracellular proteins via an induced fit or conformation selection mechanisms (Arai et al., 2015; Oldfield and Dunker, 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of resolved structures, supported by citations.

claim: Secondary structure predictions using the JPred tool support that the proximal segment of the C tail has a strong tendency to form alpha helices while the remainder of the tail is unstructured.
source: Secondary structure predictions using the JPred tool also support this view, with the proximal segment of the C tail having a strong tendency to form alpha helices while the remainder of the tail is unstructured (Drozdetskiy et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on computational predictions and a citation to Drozdetskiy et al., 2015.

claim: Numerous protein-protein interactions have been reported for ASICs that are important for channel trafficking, gating, and possibly metabotropic signaling.
source: Numerous protein-protein interactions have been reported for ASICs that are important for channel trafficking, gating, and possibly metabotropic signaling (Kellenberger and Schild, 2015; Zeng et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kellenberger and Schild, 2015 and Zeng et al., 2014.

claim: The best documented protein-protein interactions for ASICs are with PICK1, PSD-95, and stomatin.
source: The best documented of these are PICK1, PSD-95, and stomatin (Baron et al., 2002; Hruska-Hageman et al., 2004; Hruska-Hageman et al., 2002; Klipp et al., 2020; Leonard et al., 2003; Price et al., 2004; Zha et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The interaction between ASIC3's C tail and stomatin enables stomatin to inhibit channel activation through a mechanism involving the first transmembrane helix.
source: Of particular note is the interaction between ASIC3's C tail and stomatin, which enables stomatin to inhibit channel activation through a mechanism involving the first transmembrane helix (Klipp et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Klipp et al., 2020.

claim: The membrane proximal region of the ASIC1 C tail becomes liberated from the N tail during desensitization, allowing for the recruitment of RIP1 kinase.
source: In addition, recent work has suggested that the membrane proximal region of the ASIC1 C tail becomes liberated from the N tail during desensitization, allowing for the recruitment of RIP1 kinase (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2020.

claim: Activation of RIP1 by ASIC1 results in RIP1 phosphorylation leading to eventual cell death via necroptosis.
source: This results in activation of RIP1 by phosphorylation leading to eventual cell death via necroptosis.
evidence: This is supported by prior citations in the manuscript.

claim: Canonical activation of RIP1 by the tumor necrosis factor (TNF) receptor 1 (TNFR1) occurs through heterodimerization of death domains (DD) present on both RIP1 and TNFR1.
source: Canonical activation of RIP1 by the tumor necrosis factor (TNF) receptor 1 (TNFR1) occurs through heterodimerization of death domains (DD) present on both RIP1 and TNFR1 (Meng et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Meng et al., 2018.

claim: The intracellular N and C terminal tails of chicken ASIC1 are 15 and 67 amino acids, respectively.

evidence: This is a direct statement about the construct used.

claim: A clonal Human Embryonic Kidney 293T (HEK293T) cell line with the endogenous ASIC1 gene knocked out was used for all experiments.

evidence: This is a description of the experimental system, supported by a citation.

claim: The DPA molar extinction coefficient at 420 nm was determined to be 26,500 M−1cm−1.
source: The DPA molar extinction coefficient at 420 nm was determined to be 26,500 M−1cm−1 by fitting the slope of absorption measurements from serial dilutions of DPA into saline or 1% SDS.
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements.

claim: The DPA molar extinction coefficient value of 26,500 M−1cm−1 is consistent with previously reported measurements.
